Transparently between the user and the origin; origin is wherever the content really lives: an S3 bucket, a backend server, any URL (doesn't even have to be yours).
Nobody pushes; the CDN pulls: on a request for something it doesn't have, it asks the origin, keeps the answer and serves it. CDNs offer APIs, but storing content isn't their main job.

The server does no real work, just copies the same static bytes; photos are heavy (1-10 MB) and leave through the same network card every API call needs, wasting API server bandwidth ('close to a crime'); and the bytes travel from Singapore to the US on every view (distance/latency).
A CDN property: a hostname on the provider (e.g. instacdn.net) mapped to your origin (e.g. instaimages.com); just one origin URL.
Ordinary DNS: you point the CDN hostname at the CDN provider in DNS (Route 53 or any domain provider); the browser resolves the host and sends the request to the CDN's IP without knowing it's a CDN.

Browser resolves the CDN host via DNS -> CDN's IP; sends GET path to the CDN; CDN looks up the property's origin; swaps the host, keeps the path; fetches same path from the origin; caches the bytes and returns them. (Page uses instacdn.net/A/1729.png, not a.mycdn.net/system-design/logo.png.)
The host changes (CDN host -> origin host); the path stays the same (plain string replacement). The origin may include its own path prefix, e.g. instaimages.com/static.
It's a hit: served from the CDN's cached copy; the origin never hears about it, until the copy expires and one request refills.
No: to the CDN a response is just bytes - images, video, JSON; Cache-Control/cache rules decide whether and how long.
